title: The Soul of Goodness
description: Peter Vilhelm Ilsted, “A Mother and Child in an interior,” 1898, via Wikimedia Commons. The Difficulty of Virtue In his Nicomachean Ethics , in a sentence filled with insight, both anthropological and psychological, Aristotle observes, “Anyone can get angry, that is easy… but to be so with the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive, and in the right way, that is not for everyone, nor is it easy; wherefore goodness is both rare and laudable and noble.” 1 In effect, Aristotle is saying that human nature is wild and passionate, and that this natural wildness is essentially good inasmuch as it is an innate principle of actions that are themselves good, at least to the extent they can achieve goodness. However, he is also saying that our wild and passionate nature requires further formation if it is to become altogether good—“laudable and noble”—but that such formation in goodness, however dearly needed, is nevertheless terribly rare. It is so rare precisely because of the difficulty of bringing this formation to completion. This is in fact the principal positive difficulty of human life—the entirely natural challenge with which we are tasked as we proceed toward the future. It is the difficulty of receiving the gift of the goodness of our nature while simultaneously taking responsibility for the proper maturation of this nature—all so that our nature might attain its proper completion in our individual lives. This difficulty has a name; its name is virtue—for virtue is the immediate goal of this tough process of formation. Yet, while difficult, this task is most certainly worth the effort.

title: The Art of Being Good
description: Winslow Homer, “Snap the Whip,” 1872, via Wikimedia Commons . The Need for Cultivation I spent the morning watching our seven-month-old as he attempted to conquer the world—his bright eyes surveying with rapt attention, wonder exuding from every pore, muscles taut in exploration and discovery—everything in him reaching for understanding and achievement, striving toward truth and goodness. Watching our little boy, I was again reminded that our greatest drive—one might even say our primal instinct—is this inner impulsion toward truth and goodness. This powerful drive is evidently a most important feature of human life, perhaps the most important, and everything in our little boy strains forward as a result of its powerful thrust. But this drive is also wild . Wild, not in the sense of chaotic and messy, and therefore problematic, but in the entirely natural sense of not-yet-gardened. It is the wild of nature before the activity of a gardener, bold and intense, fierce and powerful—yet also good, with a goodness that is in need only of our intervention to bring it home. In the same way as the wilds of nature need a gardener to flourish, so too this interior drive requires our cultivation if it is to take its proper shape. The reason for this is found in the fact that God does not create the human (or indeed, anything) “fully made,” but rather furnishes us with an aptitude to develop over the course of time—and thereby gradually attain our natural perfection. From this we see that from the outset of our lives we are established in the privileged position of being collaborators with God in our own creation, for, as St. Thomas notes, “the dignity of causality is imparted even to creatures” by God.

title: Sobriety and Conceptual Shifts
description: Caravaggio, “Bacchus,” 1596, via Wikimedia Commons. What Does it Mean to be “Sober”? Language shifts. Sometimes the change leaves a gaping void in our ability to understand the world and our place in it. Consider, for instance, the virtue term ‘sober.’ When you hear that word, what do you envision? You might say someone is sober when you mean that he isn’t currently drunk. Or maybe you thought that someone is sober in the sense of having ‘sobered up,’ having formed a stable disposition not to partake at all in the relevant intoxicant. Sometimes such people live in a “sober house.” Or, third, you might think of someone as sober when he is solemn, mature, not prone to frivolity. Gimli the dwarf of the Lord of the Rings books—but not the movies, where he is played for comic effect—is sober. The first usage— ‘sober’ as not currently drunk—names a present state, not a stable trait. Habitual drunkards can be sober in that first sense. Of the latter two, it is only the middle that deals with intoxicants, and so only the middle that stands a chance to be the virtue of sobriety. But importantly, that second use of the term—having a stable disposition not to partake in the relevant intoxicant at all —does not express the traditional virtue of sobriety. Sobriety in the Traditional Sense To be sober , in the traditional sense, is to be a person stably disposed to partake of intoxicants in the right measure, for the right reasons, in the right occasions.
